newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-5-yr notes, thanks but no thanks.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-5-yr notes, thanks but no thanks.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market is likely to come under pressure Wednesday amid concern the $12.5 billion, five-year notes auction may draw lackluster demand at best, analysts and traders said.
"The five-year note auction could be lousy," said analyst James Padinha at MMS International.

"Who is going to buy that? The intermediate sector is too risky. The belly of the curve is too fat," added Padinha, referring to past heavy buying of intermediate U.S. securities by portfolio managers.
One trader echoed that view while predicting the five-year note auction is likely to be "again, a Street affair," with dealers absorbing the bulk of the supply in the absence of retail interest.
The trader also expected dealers to seek further price concessions ahead of the 1300 EDT/1800 GMT auction bidding deadline on Wednesday.
Hurt by uncertainty about the U.S. monetary outlook, the when-issued five-year note has already backed up a whopping 18 basis points since beginning to trade at a yield of 6.36 percent.
"I would not be surprised to see 6.60 percent come auction time," the trader cautioned.
While there are no major U.S. economic reports slated for release on Wednesday, the market may find an excuse to sell on the release of the Tankan -- the equivalent of the Beige Book.
A strong Tankan may hint at a Japanese interest rate hike that could lift the yen at the dollar's expense and be a negative for U.S. financial assets.
The trader also said the long end, which is free from supply worries, could escape relatively unscathed -- mainly since a 7.0-percent yield has proved attractive to buyers.
Padinha added that spread makes the 10-year note relatively attractive since investors have little incentive to extend the duration of their investments by 20 years for a meager additional return.
MCM MoneyWatch senior economist Astrid Adolfson expected steady buying interest in the long bond for as long as its yield remains in the neighborhood of 7.0 percent.

"That's where (7.0-percent) it (bond yield) ought to be, at least until the payrolls," said Adolfson, referring to the September 6 release of the August employment report that is expected to shed more light on the economic outlook.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York refrained from open-market operations on Tuesday, with three-day and seven-day fixed system repurchase agreements in place.
Federal funds are expected to open on target at 5.25 percent on Wednesday.
